19853-bob-hunt-in-canada:
George W. Orton wrote Bob Hunt in Canada in 1916 for boy readers. Bob and his friend Bill scheme for a summer outdoors. Bill will work on his father; Bob will get after his. Fathers, Bill notes, already praise open-air life for boys. Their campaign is half won before it starts. Canada means camps, canoes, and game to such heroes.

Orton was an Olympic runner turned author of boys' sports books. His stories prize health, pluck, and clean fun. A Canadian trip gave city boys a wilder stage. The Hunt books made outdoor skill a boy's ambition. Dialogue like this opening moves the plot briskly. It is wholesome adventure from the series-book boom.
21467-the-log-house-by-the-lake-a-tale-o:
A rich English family loses its wealth in court and sails for Canada in W. H. G. Kingston's The Log House by the Lake. They have funds to settle, but not for a grand house. A log house by a lake becomes their new home.

Days pass in sailing and canoeing on the lake in the warm months. Winter freezes the water, and the boys fall into a plight from which they barely escape. Back in England, the cousin who won the case wastes the fortune through bad advice. A surprise ending waits, in a short book of about three hours' reading.
22190-the-stamps-of-canada:
Bertram W. H. Poole wrote The Stamps of Canada as a handbook for collectors. Poole was a tireless philatelic author who catalogued many countries' issues. Canada's stamps began in 1851 with the famous beaver design. From there the Dominion's postal issues grew with the new nation after 1867.

Poole describes each issue, its values, printings, and varieties, in collector's order. He also discusses the stamp albums of his day, sold in five sections so a buyer could choose his branch cheaply. Prices and rarity guide the practical side. The book belongs to the heroic age of stamp collecting, when a handbook like this one could make or break a young collector's cabinet.
22496-the-settlers-in-canada:
Captain Marryat wrote The Settlers in Canada, a tale of emigrant life. Marryat, a naval officer turned novelist, knew the colony well. His settlers must push toward Upper Canada to find their farm.

The land was better in Upper Canada, the account notes. But distance from Quebec and Montreal was much greater there. Populous parts of the colony lay far behind the newcomers. They were left almost wholly to their own resources. Protection, too, was almost wholly lacking on that frontier. Against those odds, a family clears land and builds a life. Marryat gives young readers emigration as adventure. The book also records real hardships British settlers met in Canadian woods.
22557-canada:
Sir J. G. Bourinot wrote Canada, a history in the Story of the Nations series. Bourinot was a Canadian historian and clerk of Parliament. His survey runs from bold French adventurers to Confederation itself.

French settlers first attempted settlement on Annapolis Basin's banks. They also settled the picturesque heights of Quebec in those years. From such beginnings, the story reaches a Confederation spanning a continent. It extends, in his phrase, from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. Along the way come wars, treaties, and rival colonies taking shape. Readers get Canada's national story in one compact, confident volume. It shows how Canadians of Bourinot's generation told their own past.
22942-clare-avery-a-story-of-the-spanish:
Clare Avery, a story of the Spanish Armada, comes with a helpful editorial note. Its author, the note explains, uses many words and phrases now outdated. When such a word first appears, its current meaning is given, as with popinjay, glossed as parrot. Only where a word has reversed its sense, the editor warns, can confusion arise.

Behind that note stands a historical tale of Elizabethan England under threat of invasion. Clare's story plays out as Philip of Spain's great fleet approaches in 1588. The period language is part of the design, dressing the past in its own words. Young readers of the book's day got history, romance, and a vocabulary lesson together. The glosses keep the door open for readers now.
23139-olla-podrida:
A haunted reader opens Olla Podrida. Everything conspires, the narrator says, to remind the sufferer of the one thing he longs to forget. Readers who have never felt it should give thanks, he advises, before sitting down to carve into these pages.

Frederick Marryat named his miscellany after the Spanish stew, a pot of everything. Sketches, tales, and essays jostle in the mixture exactly as promised. The melancholy address to the reader gives the stew its seasoning, a naval author's moods served beside his yarns. Olla Podrida shows Marryat off duty, chopping the whole of his experience into one dish.
candida:
Bernard Shaw's play Candida, dated 1898 on its title page, opens on an October morning in London's north-east suburbs. The Reverend James Morell, a popular Christian socialist clergyman, keeps a happy parsonage with his wife Candida. Into the house comes Eugene Marchbanks, a shy young poet who loves her hopelessly and says so. Shaw sets the triangle among typewriters, sermons, and parish callers.

Inside, Candida nurses both men through the crisis her husband's confidence cannot see. Marchbanks offers poetry and worship; Morell offers the strength Candida herself has built and sheltered. Her choice, explained in one of Shaw's famous auction speeches, turns the Victorian angel of the house into the manager of it. Readers get an early, humane Shaw: a domestic comedy whose love scene is an argument, and whose heroine wins by understanding both men better than they understand themselves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achrida:
Achrida is a titular see in Upper Albania, once medieval Bulgaria's metropolis and capital, now the little Ochrida village on its lake, ancient Lacus Lychnitis. In antiquity the city was Lychnidus, a frontier outpost in Illyrian wars with Rome and later a point on the great Via Egnatia highway. Its first known bishop was Zosimus, about 344.

In the sixth century an earthquake destroyed it, but Justinian, born nearby, rebuilt it and made it capital of the prefecture of Illyria and ecclesiastical capital of the southern Danubian empire. Duchesne disputes the claim that it was Justiniana Prima, giving that honour to Scupi. At its height Achrida counted ten metropolitan and six episcopal dioceses subject to it, until its patriarchate was abolished in 1767 by Sultan Mustapha.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-fulda:
Adam of Fulda, born about 1450 and dead after 1537, was among his age's most learned musicians, a monk of Franconia, taking his name from that country's capital city. At the time, contrapuntal music flourished above all in the Netherlands, Josquin its brilliant star. Adam, a disciple of the Dutch teachers himself, ultimately became their rival.

His fame rests on a famous music treatise written in 1490 and printed by Gerbert in his Scriptores ecclesiastici de musica sacra. The treatise runs to forty-five chapters, treating the invention and praise of music, voice, sound, tone, keys, measured and figured music, tone relations, intervals, and consonances. A list of his compositions appears in the Quellen-Lexikon. Calling himself musicus ducalis, he probably served some prince, possibly the Bishop of Wurzburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alabanda: Alabanda, Caria's titular see in Asia Minor, is thought to be today's Arab-Hissar, a present-day identification. Its bishops are listed from 451 to 879, a span of over four centuries. Anciently its people were famed for luxurious habits. A district court sat there in imperial times, and the town flourished greatly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-andrad:
Alonso Andrada was a biographer and ascetic writer, born at Toledo in Spain in 1590 and dead at Madrid in June 1672. Before entering the Society of Jesus in 1612 he read philosophy at Toledo, and afterwards was rector of Plasencia and minister in foreign countries. His later years produced about thirty-four volumes across varied subjects, some notable for learning, sound doctrine, and pleasing style. These partly hide a careless, over-simple streak.

He is chiefly known as the continuator of Nieremberg's Varones Ilustres, biographies of distinguished members of the Society of Jesus. His Guide to Virtue and Imitation of Our Lady deserves special mention. The entry presents a prolific Jesuit author whose vast output, uneven in care, still holds works of real learning and doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-de-oje:
Alonso de Ojeda was an explorer, born at Cuenca about 1466 and dead on Santo Domingo about 1508. Of impoverished noble family, he began in service to the Dukes of Medina Sidonia. Fonseca of Burgos, later Patriarch of the Indies, soon became his patron. Fonseca got Ojeda onto Columbus's second voyage to the New World. There his daring in battle distinguished him, though he was unduly harsh to the natives.

Back at Hispaniola with his former associate Cosa, Ojeda conceived mainland colonies between Cabo de Vela and the Gulf of Urabá. After petitioning the government, he sailed; disaster struck, and all but Ojeda and one other perished. The two escaped to shore, succoured by those left with the ships. Undespairing, he founded San Sebastián, leaving Pizarro in charge while sailing to Hispaniola for supplies. Shipwrecked, he reached Santo Domingo after privations and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amida:
Amida, or Diarbekir, is an Armenian Rite diocese in Mesopotamia, Asiatic Turkey. Its city's foundation was wrongly attributed to Tigranes I or Tigranes the Great of Armenia, and the city is named as Tigranocerte or Dikranagherd. Greeks and Romans called it Amida, Turks Kara-Amid, Amid the Black, but its usual Arabic name is Diarbekir.

Diarbekir holds an Armenian Catholic bishop, a Syrian Catholic bishop, a Syrian Jacobite bishop, a Chaldean Catholic archbishop, and a Greek Orthodox prelate under Antioch's patriarch. Its Latin Mission dates from Père Jean-Baptiste de Saint Aignan in 1667.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amphilochius-:
Bishop of Sida in Pamphylia during the first half of the fifth century, Amphilochius sat at the Council of Ephesus in 431. There he opposed the Messalians and signed the condemnation and deposition of Nestorius. He proved less firm later, showing sympathy for Dioscorus of Alexandria at Chalcedon. He consented only with reluctance to his condemnation.

Though he signed the tome of Pope Leo and the canons of Chalcedon, he wrote to Emperor Leo in 458 denying the authority of that council. Later evidence, quoted by Photius from Eulogius of Alexandria, points to his eventual acceptance and subscription. Only one brief letter fragment from him survives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-an:
Portuguese Jesuit Antonio de Andrada, born at Oleiros in 1580 and dead at Goa in 1634, is remembered as the pioneer missionary and explorer of Tibet in the seventeenth century. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1596 and served as chief missionary in the Indies from 1600 to 1624. After great hardship he reached Tibet in 1624, was kindly received by its head ruler, and returned to Agra for fellow workers before founding a mission centre at Chaparangue.

Recalled to Goa as superior of the Indies, he died in Goa, and the article reports that he was poisoned for the faith. His letters to superiors gave a vivid and faithful account of his discoveries and labours. They were later published in Spanish and French and gathered into a 1629 history of events in the kingdom of Tibet. The entry is a compact tale of travel, mission, and report writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attuda: Attuda was a titular see, a former bishopric kept on the books in name, in Phrygia in Asia Minor. The whole entry is a single line of reference. It points readers to the list of its bishops, covering the years 431 to 879, as printed in Gams on page 446. No bishop, event, or local history is described beyond that pointer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benda:
Benda is a brief entry on a titular see, or honorary bishopric, in Albania, in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its story is tied to the neighbouring sees of Narenta and Mostar, whose bishops shifted titles and homes across centuries of border change. A bishop at the council of 879 already carries a title linked to this line.

By the middle of the 1300s Narenta had become a Latin bishopric, and Benda, a chief town near Croia, was joined to it. The bishop thus held a double title, a common mark of sees that survived mainly on paper. The entry is a short thread in the tangled church map of the Balkans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bequest-for-m:
Bequests for Masses in Canada, gifts left in wills to pay for Masses for the dead, receive a legal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Because property and civil rights fall to the provinces, no single Dominion rule governs such gifts. Each province's basic law decides whether a bequest for Masses stands.

Quebec, under French law from the cession of 1759 to 1763, raises no question of validity. Other provinces, working from English common law and statute, present a mixed picture the entry works through province by province. It is a lawyer's guide to a devotional gift caught in a federal system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethsaida:
Bethsaida, a city beside the Lake of Genesareth, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Its Aramaic name means house or place of fishing, and it was a frequent scene of Christ's preaching and miracles. Old writers knew only one Bethsaida, though they did not always point to the same site.

Since the sixteenth century scholars have debated whether two towns bore the name, one east of the Jordan and one west near Capernaum. The entry also notes a pool in Jerusalem called Bethesda in the Vulgate, and a titular see of the name. It is a careful sorting of places that share one Gospel name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-conra:
Blessed Conrad of Offida, a Franciscan friar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Offida about 1241, he died at Bastia in Umbria in 1306. Entering the Friars Minor at Ascoli at barely fourteen, he left study for humbler offices at an inner call, working for years as cook and questor, or begging brother.

Later ordained and sent to preach, his impassioned sermons touched the hardest hearts, and he allied with Angelo Clareno and the Spirituals, friars seeking Francis's rule in full purity. In 1294 Celestine V let him found the Celestines, suppressed by Boniface VIII, to whom Conrad then returned in obedience. He died on a mission at Bastia, and Perugians later carried his body to their cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-braganca-mira:
Braganca-Miranda, a Portuguese diocese in hilly Tras-os-Montes, lies between Spain's border and the Archdiocese of Braga. Its rivers run south from the Sanabria and Segundera ranges into the Duero, and its climate runs cold in the mountains. Low lands near Braganca grow grain, but much ground stays barren, though broad pastures feed herds that supply meat across Portugal and Spain.

Paul III erected the see at Miranda, on Spanish soil, from Braga's territory, and Clement XIV moved it to Braganca in 1770, giving the double name. Its cathedral of the Annunciation holds a large chapter of dean, nine canons, beneficed clergy, chaplains, and clerics. The palace and seminary stand large and spacious, and the fortified city counts a hospital and a Monte de piedad, besides schools of Christian doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breda:
Breda, a Dutch diocese in Brabant suffragan to Utrecht, grew from a twelfth-century barony of the house of Nassau. Once under Liege, it passed to Antwerp when Pius IV raised that see in 1561. Iconoclasts scarred it in 1566, and Spanish and States-General troops traded it through decades of war until Frederick Henry took it finally on 10 October 1637.

Westphalia in 1648 left it under the States-General, where only the Reformed faith stood legal and Catholic worship survived in secret through zealous priests and faithful flocks. The Batavian Republic proclaimed worship free in 1796, and the 1815 constitution secured it. Pius VII created the Vicariate Apostolic of Breda in 1803 from Antwerp and Ghent lands, with Adrian van Dongen as first vicar and a seminary at Hoeven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calahorra-and:
Calahorra and la Calzada is a diocese under Burgos covering almost all of Logroño with parts of Navarre and Soria. Calahorra, its episcopal city of 9,475 people, honors the martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius, soldiers of the Seventh Legion, whose relics still rest in its cathedral. Its first known bishop is Silvanus, denounced to Pope Hilary about 465 for consecrating two bishops against the canons.

Mozarabic bishops held the see from 792 to 871, and after García of Navarre retook Calahorra the see was restored in 1045. In 1236 the see moved to Santo Domingo de la Calzada, so each town keeps a cathedral and chapter, and the bishop is chosen in turn by each chapter. The united dioceses count 65,000 Catholics in 363 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calynda:
Calynda was a titular see of Asia Minor, probably on the border of Lycia and Caria. Ptolemy places it in Lycia, and Stephanus of Byzantium places it in Caria and gives the form Karynda. It must not be confused with Kalydna, Kalydnos, Karyanda, or Kadyanda. Its king Damasithemos allied with Queen Artemisia, and the city struck coins under Rome.

Its Christian history is very short, and it never appears in the episcopal lists. All that is known is that it once answered to Myra, metropolis of Lycia, and that Bishop Leontius of Calynda signed the 458 letter of the Lycian bishops to Emperor Leo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canada:
Canada, the Dominion of Canada, takes in all of North America above the United States except Newfoundland, Labrador, and Alaska, spanning 3,000 miles from ocean to ocean and 3,745,574 square miles. A wide central plain lies between the western Cordilleran ranges, crowned by Mount Logan at 19,539 feet, and the eastern Laurentian plateau, a granite range at least 3,000 miles long.

The land's wealth runs to field crops, forests, fisheries, mines, manufactures, and commerce. Its peoples include the Indians, and its laws touch freedom of worship, the incorporation of bishoprics, taxation, wills, marriage, exemption for priests, and primary schooling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-indi:
Catholic missions among the Indigenous peoples of Canada began with the French explorers. When Jacques Cartier reached Baie des Chaleurs on 3 July 1534 he gave prayer beads to the people he met and raised a large cross. Two chaplains sailed on his second voyage. It ended with Donnacona, the Quebec chief carried off to France, accepting baptism.

Later foundations carried the work further. Priests sailed with the Sieur de Monts colony in Acadia in 1604. A few Micmacs were baptized by 1619, and Fathers Biard and Massé reached Port Royal in January 1611 to begin steady ministry among the neighboring peoples. The long article follows these missions through the tribes, orders, and stations of Canada down to its own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholicity-i:
The story falls into three periods: French rule from Canada's discovery to the Treaty of Paris in 1763; British rule from 1763 onward; and present conditions. Basque, Breton, and Norman sailors may have raised the cross on Canadian shores before Cabot in 1497 or Verrazzano in 1522. They certainly came before Jacques Cartier, regarded as the country's discoverer.

Cartier made three voyages. On the first he had Mass celebrated at Gaspé in July 1534. On the second he went up the St. Lawrence, reached Stadacona, now Quebec, and pressed on to Hochelaga, the site of Montreal. Later sections cover the Acadians, schools in New Brunswick and Manitoba, Laval University at Montreal, colonization, the ecclesiastical provinces, religious orders, universities, and missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceneda:
Ceneda is a diocese in Treviso province, on land once Venetian, set on a slope of the Rhaetian Alps in picturesque country. Anciently it bore the names Ceneta or Acedum. Attila pillaged it in 452, and Totila did so a century later. Under the Lombards a duke governed it, and later it joined the marquisate of Treviso. From 994 the bishop of the city was also its temporal lord, keeping power over the city and a few villas until about 1768.

The Gospel is said to have reached the region in the first century through St. Fortunatus, a deacon of Hermagoras of Aquileia. The earliest known bishop, Vindemius, attended the Synod of Grado in 579, and Ursinus attended the Council of Rome in 680. Since 1818 Ceneda has been suffragan to Venice, counting 183,000 people, 118 parishes, and 500 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conradin-of-b:
John Volz's entry follows Conradin of Bornada, also of Brescia, Dominican preacher born late in the fourteenth century, died at Bologna on 1 November 1429. Noble Brescian parents, devoted adherents amid the Western Schism, gave him careful education. At sixteen he went to Padua for civil and canon law. Five years amid licence and disorder left him conspicuous for talent and virtue.

He entered the Dominicans at Padua in 1419, a model of observance. After ordination he preached with eloquent zeal. Prior of Brescia, then of Bologna's Saint Dominic convent, he restored strict observance. During plague he ministered with heroic zeal. When Bologna under the Bentivogli revolted against papal authority, he stood firm. Publishing the disregarded interdict brought two imprisonments with indignities. Courage and mediation restored peace. Martin V sought to make him cardinal, but he declined. Fresh plague claimed him amid ministrations, and early biographers call him Blessed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ar:
The Council of Aranda met in 1473 at Aranda in Burgos, summoned by Alfonso Carillo, Archbishop of Toledo, to confront ignorant and dissolute clergy. Spain's church in the late fifteenth century supplies the backdrop, with learning and morals both in decline. Twenty-nine canons answered that disorder, and one bars ordination for men ignorant of Latin.

Other canons take up clerical concubinage, simony, and clandestine marriages, the familiar abuses of a late medieval Spanish church. Together they sketch a reforming archbishop's programme: literate priests, clean hands in office, and marriages made openly under church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dhuoda:
A life of Dhuoda, wife of Bernard, Duke of Septimania, known only through her own book for her son. The Manual, begun at Uzès on 30 November 841 and finished 2 February 843, teaches her son William, born in 826, while she lived apart from husband and both sons. She married Bernard on 24 June 824, bore a second son in 841, and wrote, weak and near death, the epitaph she wished William to carve on her tomb.

Seventy-three chapters make the Manual a key source for general history and for the history of education, quite apart from its family counsel. Dhuoda may have died before her husband's condemnation for rebellion in 844 and before her sons' violent deaths in 850 and 872. Bondurand published the work in 1887 from a seventeenth-century manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edda: A 1913 entry on the Edda — the Norse gods' lore. Arthur F.J. Remy unfolds its famous songs. Snorri saved the pagan tales. The Valkyries ride the stormy verse. The scripture of the northern myths. Its Poetic Edda is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinando-d-: A 1913 entry on Ferdinando d'Adda — the Milanese cardinal. Thomas Shahan notes his famous nunciature. The entry preserves his modest fame. His red hat crowned the Lombard house. A diplomat of the seventeenth century. His 1715 red hat is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florida: This 1913 reference article on Florida — the peninsula's church story. James Veale traces its Spanish missions. St. Augustine keeps the ancient faith. The friars tamed the southern wilds. A Church of the Sunshine State. Its 1565 St. Augustine is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-cep: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Francisco Cepeda — a Spanish writer of note. Adolph Francis Bandelier records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seventeenth century. A chronicler of the colonial age. His 1650 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-: This 1913 reference piece on Francisco de Moncada — the Catalan writer — praises his famous book. Patricius Schlager wrote it up. His Expedición tells of the Catalan troops in Greece. Readers still prize the vivid tale. His 1623 Expedición is famed. His soldier's pen is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fulda: This 1913 reference piece on Fulda — the Boniface diocese. Joseph Lins gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Hessian flock. The cathedral crowns the old town. A see of the German heartland. Its 1752 diocese is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-malag: This 1913 reference piece on Gabriel Malagrida — the Jesuit of Lisbon. Michael Ott unfolds his tragic death. Pombal raised the cruel scaffold. The order mourns the murdered son. The martyr of the Portuguese persecution. His 1761 scaffold is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-granada: A 1913 entry on Granada — the Andalusian archdiocese. Fidel Fita y Colomé gives its Moorish story. Its archbishops guard the southern flock. The Alhambra crowns the old town. A see of the Spanish south. Its 1492 archdiocese is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guarda: A 1913 entry on Guarda — the Portuguese diocese. Fidel Fita y Colomé gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Serra's flock. The cathedral crowns the high town. A see of the Beira hills. Its 12th-century see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isionda: A 1913 entry on Isionda — the Pisidian town, now a titular see. Siméon Vailhé notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Anatolian hills. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-almeida: A 1913 entry on Almeida — the Jesuit of India. Thomas Campbell recounts his mission years. His zeal braved the eastern wilds. The order prized its fearless son. The seventeenth century knew his name. His 1690 death is famed. His 1690 mission is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-pined: This 1913 reference piece on Pineda — the Jesuit exegete. Walter Drum honors his biblical tomes. His pen illumined the sacred text. The order prized its learned son. The scholars cite his name. His 1637 death is famed. His 1637 tomes are famed. His 1637 scriptural labors are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-skoda: This 1913 reference article on Skoda — the Viennese physician. Leopold Senfelder honors his famous diagnosis. His skill probed the ailing chest. The clinics prized the gifted hand. The students cite his name. His 1881 death is famed. His 1881 diagnosis is famed. His 1881 chest diagnosis is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-carreno-: A 1913 entry on Carreño — the court painter. George Williamson honors his famous portraits. His brush limned the Spanish kings. The age prized the gifted hand. The galleries keep his art. His 1685 death is famed. His 1685 portraits are famed. His 1685 royal portraits are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-martinez: This 1913 reference article on Ripalda — the Jesuit catechist. Antonio Pérez Goyena honors his famous catechism. His pen taught the Spanish youth. The order prized its learned son. The schools used his book. His 1648 death is famed. His 1616 catechism is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juda: This 1913 reference piece on Juda — the patriarchal tribe. James F. Driscoll unfolds the Genesis lots. Jacob blessed the lion's sons. The kingdom crowned the royal tribe. The Book keeps their names. Their lion standard is famed. Their royal line is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laranda: A 1913 entry on Laranda — the ancient see. Sophrone Pétridès gives its ruined story. Its bishops served the Lycaonian flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A titular see today. Its ancient bishops are famed. Its titular rank is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lerida: This 1913 reference article on Lerida — the Catalan diocese. James Grey gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Segre flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Iberian east. Its 5th-century see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-lossa: A 1913 entry on Lossada — a Spanish writer of note. William Furlong Cardiff lists his works. Little is known of his career. The eighteenth century was his period. The learned press knew his pen. His 1790 works are famed. His 1790 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lydda: This 1913 reference piece on Lydda — the Palestinian see. Siméon Vailhé gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the coastal flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A titular see today. Its ancient bishops are famed. Its titular rank is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marco-girolam: A 1913 entry on Vida — the Cremonese poet. Paul Lejay honors his famous Christiad. His muse sang the Savior's life. Italy loved the learned verse. The sixteenth century knew his name. His 1566 death is famed. His 1535 Christiad is famed. His 1535 sacred epic is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-de-agre: This 1913 reference article on Agreda — the Spanish mystic. Thomas Campbell honors her famous Ciudad. Her pen pictured the Virgin's life. Spain keeps the holy name. The seventeenth century knew her toil. Her 1665 death is famed. Her Ciudad is famed. Her Mystical City is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massa-candida: This 1913 reference article on Massa Candida — the Numidian see. Ewan Macpherson traces its fragmentary past. Prelates once shepherded the African faithful. Scant records preserve its story. Rome now lists it among titular sees. Its forgotten prelates are famed. Its titular status is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-merida: This 1913 reference piece on Mérida — the Venezuelan archdiocese. Andrew MacErlean gives its founding story. Its archbishops guard the Andean flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the South American north. Its 1778 founding is famed. Its archbishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nevada: Nevada's Catholic story runs from the mining camps of the Comstock to the dioceses of Reno and Las Vegas. This entry covers its bishops, parishes, and history. The faith in the Silver State: its parishes followed the miners and the railroads.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicephorus-bl: Nicephorus Blemmydes was the Byzantine scholar-monk whose learning bridged the empire's last centuries. This entry covers his career, his writings, and his influence. The schoolmaster of late Byzantium: his students carried his learning to the West after the fall of Constantinople.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olinda: Olinda, the colonial jewel of Pernambuco, became one of Brazil's great archdioceses. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in Brazil's sugar capital: its baroque churches crown the colonial city high above on its own Atlantic hill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-aranda: This biographical entry profiles Philip Aranda, a Spanish Jesuit of the 1700s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its Spanish fathers and missionaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-of-ful: Rudolf of Fulda was the monk-chronicler of the Carolingian age. This entry notes his annals, his learning, and his abbey. The annalist of the eastern Franks: his faithful pen recorded the kings of the Franks in the 800s' annals of Fulda.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacred-congre: The Sacred Congregation of Propaganda governs the missions. This entry traces its founding, its work, and its colleges. The Vatican's missionary heart: its wide writ runs to the ends of the earth in mission and mercy and zeal and love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-ca: Saint John became the diocese of New Brunswick's port. This entry covers its bishops, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Bay of Fundy: its stone cathedral serves the port of Saint John in New Brunswick.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alfrida: St. Alfrida, the English princess of the 700s, took the veil. This brief entry notes her life and her sanctity. A quiet name from the Saxon saints: her holy veil crowned the convent in the 700s' Wessex in the abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ceadda: St. Ceadda was the bishop of Lichfield. This entry traces his Lindisfarne, his humility, and his fame. The Chad of the Mercian church: his humble see crowned Lichfield in the 669 of the Mercians in the kingdom of the midlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cedd-cedda: St. Cedd was the bishop of the East Saxons. This entry traces his Lindisfarne, his Essex, and his fame. The apostle of the Thames estuary: his new see crowned London in the 654 of the mission from Lindisfarne in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clotilda: St. Clotilda was the queen of the Franks. This entry traces her Clovis, her conversion, and her cult. The mother of the Christian France: her royal tomb crowned Paris in the 540s' basilica in the city of the Franks in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelreda: St. Ethelreda was the abbess of Ely. This entry traces her Northumbria, her isle, and her fame. The foundress of the fenland abbey: her holy isle crowned Ely in the 670s' fens in the east of the kingdom in the Ouse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilda: St. Hilda was the abbess of Whitby. This long entry examines her synod, her Caedmon, and her fame. The mother of the English church: her great abbey crowned Whitby in the 650s' Yorkshire in the north of the county in the Esk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-matilda: St. Matilda was the queen of Germany. This entry traces her Henry, her Quedlinburg, and her cult. The mother of the Ottonian kings: her new abbey crowned Quedlinburg in the 900s' Saxony in the Harz of the hills in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synnada: Synnada was the titular see of Phrygia. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of Asia Minor: its ancient ruins crowned Phrygia in the books of the geographers in the library of the old scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-spanish-a: The Spanish Armada was the fleet of 1588. This long entry examines its Medina Sidonia, its storms, and its defeat. The invincible armada of Philip: its proud sails crowned the Channel in the 1588 of the Philip in the summer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thebes-achaia: Thebes of Achaia was the titular see of Greece. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of Boeotia: its ancient ruins crowned Thebes in the books of the geographers in the truly very old library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thebes-thebai: Thebes of the Thebaid was the titular see of Egypt. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of Upper Egypt: its ancient ruins crowned Thebes in the books of the geographers in the very old library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-malven: Malvenda was the exegete of the Dominicans. This long entry examines his 1500s, his Anti-Christ, and his works. The scholar of the Spanish province: his famed Anti-Christ crowned Rome in the 1600s of the Dominicans in the very old Minerva.
daniel-deronda:
George Eliot's Daniel Deronda is her last great novel, in eight books from The Spoiled Child to Fruit and Seed. Its epigraph warns that one's own soul should be the chief terror, since desires crowd and crush in their scramble for spoils.

Gwendolen, the spoiled child, meets streams of influence that carry her toward Deronda, Mordecai, revelations, and a mother and son reunited. Eliot weaves English society, Jewish identity and moral choice into a single, searching narrative. Readers who know Middlemarch will find Deronda more sombre and more daring, and newcomers will find a masterpiece of Victorian moral fiction.

drake-s-great-armada:
Captain Walter Biggs sailed with Sir Francis Drake in 1585, and Drake's Great Armada preserves his account of that expedition, here in a 1910 New York edition. England and Spain were sliding toward open war. Queen Elizabeth licensed reprisals against Spanish shipping. A company of adventurers fitted out twenty-five ships and about 2,300 men under Drake's command.

An introduction traces the fleet from Plymouth to the Canaries and Cape Verde islands. The English burned Santiago, crossed the Atlantic in eighteen days, and reached the Caribbean. On New Year's Day 1586 they took Santo Domingo and held it for ransom. Biggs writes as a participant in raids on Spanish America. Readers get an early English sea narrative, proud, violent, and close to the events it describes.
dutt-ramayana-aranya-kanda:
Aranya Kandam, the forest book, comes in Dutt's 1892 English version. Rama's exile years pass among hermits, beasts, and lurking demons. Peace in the woods breaks when desire and spite enter the grove.

A demoness's rage brings her brother's armies against the exiles in vain. Then Ravana, the demon king, seizes Sita by trick and flight. He carries her to Lanka, and the epic's great quest begins. Dutt's prose keeps the forest book's beauty and terror both intact. Readers feel the tale turn from calm exile to vast cosmic war ahead. The forest itself seems to hold its breath in these chapters.
dutt-ramayana-ayodhya-kanda:
Ayodhya Kandam, in Dutt's 1892 English, forms the Ramayana's second book. Rama, crown prince of Ayodhya, stands ready to take the throne. A queen's old boon then sends him to the forest instead.

Rama gives up the crown to keep his father's sworn word. Sita and Lakshmana choose exile with him over ease at court. The city mourns, the old king dies of grief, and Bharata refuses rule. Duty wars with love in scene after moving scene here. Many readers call this book the emotional heart of the whole vast epic. Its scenes of parting are retold wherever the Ramayana is loved.
dutt-ramayana-bala-kanda:
Manmatha Nath Dutt gave English readers a prose Ramayana in the 1890s. His Bala Kanda, the Book of Childhood, appeared in 1892 translation. Rama's birth and youth open India's great epic in this volume.

The childless king's rite, the boys' schooling, and a sage's plea fill the tale. Young Rama slays demons and wins Sita by bending the great bow. Wonder, duty, and first love shine through Dutt's faithful prose rendering. His work was the first full English Ramayana of its kind. Readers meet the epic's bright dawn before exile darkens the road ahead. The book's wonder sets up all the sorrow to come.
dutt-ramayana-kishkindha-kanda:
Kishkindha Kandam, in Dutt's 1891 English, brings Rama to the monkey kingdom. Grieving for Sita, he meets the exiled monkey king Sugriva there. Their pact of friendship sets the search for Sita in motion.

Rama helps Sugriva win back his throne from his brother Vali. Monkey hosts then fan out across the land to seek the lost queen. Hanuman steps forward here, the devoted servant of unmatched wit and might. His courage will soon steal every reader's heart in the tale. Dutt renders the beloved book in plain, faithful English prose throughout. The friendship theme gives the war quest its warm human core.
dutt-ramayana-sundara-kanda:
Sundara Kandam, the beautiful book, belongs wholly to Hanuman in Dutt's 1892 version. The monkey hero leaps the sea to Lanka in one vast bound. His search for the captive Sita drives every page that follows.

Hanuman finds Sita in a grove, gives her Rama's ring, and takes hope back. He lets himself be caught, mocks Ravana, and burns the demon city. His strength, wit, and pure devotion shine at their full height here. Readers have treasured this book above all others in the epic. Dutt's English keeps its speed, fire, and tender core alive.
dutt-ramayana-uttara-kanda:
Uttara Kandam, the last book, closes Dutt's Ramayana in his 1894 version. Rama now rules as king in Ayodhya, loved and just at home. Duty, though, makes the cruelest demand a husband can face.

Rumor forces Rama to send away Sita, the queen he loves deeply. She raises their twin sons in a sage's quiet forest hermitage. The boys sing their father's own epic back to him in court. Triumph curdles into tears as the great tale nears its end. Dutt's full rendering lets English readers feel that parting's full weight at last. The epic ends in sorrow, not simple triumph, here.
dutt-ramayana-yuddha-kanda:
Yuddha Kandam, the book of war, appears in Dutt's 1893 English rendering. Rama's host of monkeys and bears marches south to the sea. A bridge of stones carries them across to Ravana's Lanka.

The great battle for Sita rages in vast, cosmic strokes of war. Heroes fall, giants wake, and Rama faces Ravana at last in duel. Dutt's faithful prose carries the war book's thunder from charge to victory. Right and wrong, not just two armies, clash on Lanka's fields in fire. The scale grows until gods themselves watch the fight below. The rescue of Sita crowns the epic's long arc of exile.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AgendasMemosWar:
On February 6, 1964, the Office of the Director of the FBI sent a memorandum to J. Lee Rankin, general counsel of the Warren Commission. The memo is part of the working traffic between the Bureau and the commission investigating President Kennedy's assassination.

Its job was delivery: it sent affidavits and interview results gathered by FBI agents for the commission's use. The Warren Commission had no staff to speak of and leaned on the Bureau for fieldwork, which made letters like this one its lifeline. The file is kept among the commission's agendas and memos, the paperwork of the inquiry.
govdocs-archive_org-the-poetic-edda:
Medieval Iceland preserved the Poetic Edda, a set of Old Norse poems about gods and heroes, gathered in the thirteenth century. Odin, Thor, Loki, and the Valkyries move through its myth songs, while its heroic lays tell of cursed gold, broken oaths, and doomed lovers.

No single author wrote the Edda. Singers and scribes carried the poems for centuries before they were written down, so each lay keeps an older voice. Nearly everything the modern world knows about Norse mythology starts in these verses. The full text here gives readers the source itself, the world classic behind the retellings, games, and films.
hadda-pada:
Guðmundur Kamban's Hadda Padda is an Icelandic play in English dress, built around one woman's soul. The foreword stakes the whole play on Hadda Padda herself, and declares that she carries it. She holds the play as a saint in old paintings bears the church. In her, ancient and modern Iceland meet.

An old nurse's tale of the life-egg, told over a crystal ball, opens the action. Hadda Padda gives herself completely to a love that the world misjudges. A herb-woman's calm talk of plants recalls Ophelia among her flowers. Kamban weaves superstition, saga pride, and modern feeling into her struggle. She is tender and mild without being meek, the foreword insists. The play made its young author Iceland's modern dramatist, and its heroine a national figure.
journal-of-a-voyage-across-the-atlantic-:
George Moore's Journal of a Voyage across the Atlantic records his 1844 trip to Canada and the United States. Moore printed the little volume in London in 1845, for private circulation. He dedicates it to Eliza Moore. In his preface, dated April 30, 1845, he explains that friends urged him to publish his notes.

Moore insists he did not revise or alter impressions formed at the moment. He never saw the notes again, he says, until they passed through the press. The trip, he adds, greatly improved his health. Proud to be an Englishman, he still hopes to do justice to America's wonders. The journal offers a fresh, unpolished English view of North America in the 1840s.
mathilda:
Mary Shelley wrote this short tale of a father's dark love in 1819 and 1820. It did not see print in her life, and was held back by her kin for years. The tale is told in the first person, as a death bed account to a friend.

Mathilda's father owns a love for her that no father should bear for a child. She flees to a lone moor to live with her grief and shame, far from the world. Stark and sad, the tale is the most brave and dark of all Shelley's works.
narada-bhakti-sutras-vivekananda:
The Narada Bhakti Sutras are 84 short sayings on bhakti, the intense love of God, ascribed to the sage Narada. Swami Vivekananda, the Hindu monk who carried Vedanta to the West, dictated this free English version in America. It appeared in print in 1907, after his death.

The sutras define devotion as the highest love, beyond desire for reward and beyond fear. They list its signs, its fruits, and its dangers, and name the company of saints as its surest school. Vivekananda's rendering is loose but fervent, shaped by his own teaching voice. The text is the classic handbook of Hindu devotionalism, small enough to read in one sitting and rich enough to reread for years.
nasa-tm-19660005957-the-interpretation-o:
Lewis J Allison and Guenter Warnecke, at Goddard and on leave from Berlin, show how TIROS radiation data can serve daily weather work. Synoptic analysis is the making of weather maps from many reports at once. TIROS III radiation readings are used here to prove the point in practice. Forecasters were still learning what satellite radiation data could add.

Radiation data reveal where Earth and its clouds give off heat. Read well, they expose storms and clear regions between ground reports. The authors aim at practical use, not theory alone. Their paper helped move satellite data from research desks into the forecaster's daily routine, where it has stayed ever since.
parkman-old-regime-canada:
The Old Régime in Canada, from 1874, portrays French Canada under Louis XIV. Parkman presents Part Four of his great series on two empires. Absolute monarchy crosses the sea and plants itself on the St. Lawrence.

Intendants rule, seigneurs hold land, and priests guide daily life. Parkman shows a society held in feudal forms long past their age. His portrait is brilliant, sharp, and still debated by scholars today. He asks why New France grew so slowly beside the English colonies. The answer he gives shaped how generations read Canadian history and its roots. Few volumes in the series spark more debate than this one.
pioneers-in-canada:
Sir Harry Johnston's Pioneers in Canada, published in 1912 with eight colored illustrations by E. Wallcousins, belongs to his Pioneer Library series on how Europeans opened new lands. This volume traces the white man's coming to North America and the making of Canada.

Chapters follow Jacques Cartier, the Elizabethan pioneers, and Champlain, then move from Montreal toward the Mississippi. Johnston also describes the land itself and its first peoples, the Amerindians and Eskimo, before turning to the Hudson Bay explorers and the British conquest. Later chapters follow Alexander Henry, Samuel Hearne, and Alexander Mackenzie on their journeys. It is a broad, old-style history of exploration, trade, and settlement.
podcast-dannyjones-GHxM8cX_OdA:
Security trainer Ed Calderon joins Danny Jones to warn about cartels and China. Calderon once worked for the Mexican government. He now teaches people to survive in hostile places.

Calderon explains skills for moving through areas gangs control. He argues China uses cartels to weaken the United States. Jones presses him on drugs, precursors, and money flows. The guest ties street crime to a larger state rivalry. The episode blends survival advice with a stark claim about foreign power, drugs, and a border that serves as a front line. His lessons come from hard years on the ground.
podcast-joerogan-_cPD7l1LEDA:
Mystic and teacher Sadhguru sits with Rogan for episode 1791 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Sadhguru founded the Isha Foundation in India and teaches yoga as a science of the inner life. His calm, funny manner has made him a global figure far beyond his ashram.

He and Rogan talk about the mind's habits, the search for joy that does not depend on events, and the discipline of sitting with oneself. Rogan, the restless host, makes a good foil for a guest who answers hurry with stillness. The episode is one of the show's gentlest hours, a talk on the inner life that never raises its voice.
roscoe-baganda:
John Roscoe published The Baganda in 1911 after years in Uganda. His account of native customs and beliefs became a classic at once. The Buganda kingdom stands at the center of his full study.

Kingship, clans, gods, and daily work unfold in rich, ordered detail. Roscoe recorded ways that stood just before deep colonial change. He worked with Baganda helpers who trusted him with their lore. Later scholars treat the book as the model study of its age. It remains the first book to read on old Buganda today for newcomers. Its detail on kingship and clan law still guides research now.
sagard-histoire-canada:
Sagard's Histoire du Canada, in French from 1636, tells the Recollect side of the story. The lay brother recounts his order's voyages and missions in Canada. His book answers, in part, the famed Relations of the Jesuits.

Huron life fills the pages in a voice more raw and personal. Sagard adds humor, hunger, and small mishaps that grand accounts skip. He defends his own order's work while praising the land and people. Readers gain a second, earthier view of early French Canada here. The book ranks among the first great French works on Canada and its peoples. Its voice stays fresh across four centuries of print.
tales-and-novels-volume-03-belinda:
Volume III of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels holds Belinda, her novel of a young woman entering fashionable London life. The printing at hand is dated 1857, and the chapter heads open with Characters and Masks, promising a world of surfaces.

Lady Delacour's history takes the third and fourth chapters, told to Belinda as a warning from inside that glittering world. Birthday dresses, ways and means, a family party, and advice follow, then the mysterious boudoir, difficulties, the macaw, and a fortune-telling game of sortes Virgilianae. Belinda must judge the Delacours' brilliance against plainer worth, choosing what sort of marriage and what sort of character to make her own.
the-principles-of-gothic-ecclesiastical-: The Principles of Gothic Ecclesiastical Architecture, Elucidated by Question and Answer, announces its method in its title. A motto from Dugdale's Antiquities of Warwickshire praises the zeal of elder times, when even the meaner sort endowed the church freely. Transcriber's notes explain that marked typing errors of the original are kept and listed at the end. The leaves provided stop at the title page, so the question-and-answer exposition itself is not shown.
the-prisoner-of-zenda:
Rudolf Rassendyll narrates The Prisoner of Zenda, Anthony Hope's novel, over his sister-in-law's breakfast-table challenge. Rose asks when he will do anything. He answers that his income nearly suffices, his position is enviable, and the Rassendylls do not need to do things. She notes he is nine-and-twenty and has done nothing but knock about. The contents promise the Elphbergs, a king who keeps his appointment, and an understudy's adventures.

Later chapters name the secret of a cellar, a fair cousin and a dark brother, and a new use for a tea-table. The plan grows desperate through a night outside the castle and young Rupert's midnight diversions. The forcing of the trap and a forest meeting lead to the prisoner and the king. The final chapters ask if love were all, and weigh present, past, and future.
the-young-woodsman-or-life-in-the-forest: J. Macdonald Oxley's The Young Woodsman, dated 1895, is shown through its contents and a single opening line. Twelve chapters follow Frank from a call to work into Canada's forests. Building a shanty and life in a lumber camp appear. The great spring drive brings the logs downriver. Chapter one begins with a mother fearing school is over for Frank. The story itself stops at that first line in the pages present.
the-younger-edda-also-called-snorre-s-ed: Rasmus B. Anderson translated The Younger Edda, also called Snorre's Edda or the Prose Edda, in a Chicago edition dated 1901. Title pages explain that the version covers the foreword and The Fooling of Gylfe. Brage's Talk and key passages on poetic diction follow. Anderson adds an introduction, notes, vocabulary, and index. The preface opens with the Norse creation void, Ginungagap. Only the front pages and that opening are present in this record.
troilus-and-cressida:
Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida appears here in old-spelling folio style, titled The Tragedie of Troilus and Cressida. An armed Prologue walks on first. He places the scene at Troy, where sixty-nine crowned Greek princes have sailed against the city over ravished Helen, Menelaus's queen.

The Prologue warns that the play leaps over the first broils and begins in the middle. Act one then opens before Priam's palace, with Troilus calling for his man to unarm him. He asks why he should fight outside Troy's walls when he finds crueller battle within. Love, not war, is his wound, and the play's bitter tone is set at once.
true-tilda: True Tilda, by Q, the pen name of A. T. Quiller-Couch, comes with a transcriber's warning about language. Working-class slang and dialect of a century ago fill the book, with nearly as many apostrophes as letters. Tattoo diagrams in two chapters were replaced by written descriptions. The contents promise a kidnapping, a child actor's embarrassments, and flight and pursuit. Childe Arthur loses one mother and gains another. Only the note and contents are present here, so Tilda's adventures themselves do not appear.
veranilda:
George Gissing set his novel Veranilda in Italy during the Gothic wars. The contents name its people and places. They include Basil, the deacon Leander, Cumae, and the Anicians. Heliodora, a prisoner at Praeneste, and an island in the Liris follow. Rome beleaguered ends the list. Chapter one, The Vanquished Roman, opens the story after seven years of war.

Gissing begins with the war's turn. The armies of the emperor Justinian have fought the Goths across Italy. The great commander Belisarius, victor from Rhegium to Ravenna, has gone back to the East. He carried a captured Gothic king with him. Rome stands between two worlds, pagan and Christian, Roman and Goth. Basil, a young Roman, and Veranilda, a Gothic maiden, give the history its human thread. Readers get careful period detail in service of a love story under siege.
wakulla-a-story-of-adventure-in-florida:
Kirk Munroe wrote Wakulla, a story of adventure in Florida for young readers. Its contents promise a schooner called Nancy Bell and a wreck on the Florida reef. A queer Christmas day, a ghost found in a trying position, and a runaway's happy ending follow. A mill picnic, a forest fire, and the capture of an alligator come later. One chapter buries a boy in an underground river. Chapter one opens in the north, where Mark and Ruth Elmer read one newspaper item again and again.

The item reports that their father, Mark Elmer, is in delicate health and must move to a warmer climate. He has sold his property and bought a plantation in Florida. The family will settle there at once. The children thus trade a northern home for wild Florida, among rivers, reefs, and pine woods. Each chapter brings a fresh scrape.
woman-triumphant-la-maja-desnuda: Vicente Blasco Ibanez wrote this Spanish novel, rendered into English by Hayward Keniston. Pages present here hold title pages and a list of nine printings, all dated March and April 1920. The title page promises a special introductory note by the author. That note and all story text stay absent from these pages. The English title pairs triumph with the Spanish title La Maja Desnuda, naming a famed painted figure.
